title: Freddie Keppard's refusal to record and the Scissor Grinder
summary: Hightower compares his own guarded playing to Keppard, who recorded only one number, 'Scissor Grinder', fearing others would steal his ideas.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Yeah, we got all the greatest bands you want to hear. That was a really a good band. They were really great. And we got along pretty good, but most of those fellows, as we will get back to myself about recording and numbers recording, I'm something like Freddie Kepler was if you never heard about it. I heard he wouldn't play or nothing. Anybody around going to catch anything? He laid it on down and he said, go on about your business, you ain't going to steal nothing from me. See? Well, that's the way I was. And then where else we'd go at night and somebody would say so-and-so, and they'd ask her, they asked my wife, tell your husband to play so-and-so. I said, no, there'll be no playing. I laid it on down. See? Until they gone. And when they gone, then I'd play. Well, that's the way Freddie Kepler was. I doubt whether Freddie Kepler made over one number, and that number was, can't think of it right now, but he wrote, he published, he let him publish that number with Charlie Cook's band in Patty Harmon's Dreamer. It's one number. The other side, they had to put another number on there. He just had one number. Oh, yeah.
There was one that's called Messin' Around.
Scissors Grinder. Yeah. Sure, yeah, I have that number. What is that? The Scissors Grinder. You know, the scissors. Scissors! That was the number. That was the number. That was the number.
